sources.title: Chapter 1 - Global Warming of 1.5 C

say.text: Welcome to class 62. Today we reach the years that many of us have lived through: 2008 to today.

show.text: 2008 to Today

say.text: We will look at five stories: the 2008 money crisis, smartphones and social media, climate change, COVID-19, and artificial intelligence. Then we ask why recent history is hard to judge.

show.text:
1. The 2008 financial crisis
2. Smartphones and social media
3. Climate change
4. COVID-19
5. Artificial intelligence
Then: why is recent history hard to judge?

say.text: First, money. A financial crisis is when banks and investors panic and stop lending to each other. The 2008 crisis started in the United States and spread around the world.

show.text: Financial crisis

say.text: In spring 2008, a bank called Bear Stearns was bought by JPMorgan Chase, with help from the Federal Reserve. On 15 September 2008, another investment bank, Lehman Brothers, filed for bankruptcy.

show.text: Spring 2008: Bear Stearns bought by JPMorgan Chase | 15 September 2008: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy

say.text: The next day, the Fed approved a loan of up to 85 billion dollars to AIG, a giant insurer. After Lehman failed, a big money fund also lost value, and the panic spread to other funds.

show.text:
16 Sept 2008: Fed lends up to $85 billion to AIG
After Lehman: a money market fund loses value
The run spreads to other money funds

ask.q: Which firm filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008?
wrong: Bear Stearns
AIG
JPMorgan Chase
ask.why: Bear Stearns was bought by JPMorgan Chase, AIG got a Fed loan, and Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy.

say.text: Many people call the slump that followed the Great Recession, and date it from Lehman's bankruptcy. But experts still argue about how much Lehman itself mattered.

show.text: Often said: the Great Recession dates from Lehman's bankruptcy | Also said: the trouble began in 2007, and Lehman's importance is disputed

say.text: The Fed's chair, Ben Bernanke, said the Fed could not lend to Lehman safely. He said there was not enough good collateral to be sure a loan would be repaid.

show.text: The Fed's explanation: not enough collateral of good quality to protect a loan to Lehman.

say.text: Next, phones. A smartphone is a phone that runs apps and connects to the internet. Social media means apps and sites where people share posts, photos and messages.

show.text: Smartphone

say.text: Pew Research Center surveys US adults. In its first smartphone survey, in 2011, 35 percent owned one. Today it is 91 percent.

show.text: Share of US adults who own a smartphone

say.text: That is about nine in every ten US adults. These figures cover the United States only.

show.text: About 9 in every 10 US adults own a smartphone

say.text: Phones also matter for access. Pew says 16 percent of US adults are smartphone dependent: they have a smartphone but no home broadband. In 2013 it was 8 percent.

show.text: 16% (up from 8% in 2013)

ask.q: In Pew's survey, what does smartphone dependent mean?
ask.right: Having a smartphone but no home broadband
wrong: Never being able to put the phone down
Owning more than one smartphone
Having no phone at all
ask.why: Pew counts people as smartphone dependent if they have a smartphone but do not subscribe to home broadband.

say.text: Now a debate. Many people worry that social media harms teenagers' mental health. In December 2023, a National Academies committee reviewed the research.

show.text: Does social media harm teenagers?

say.text: It found not enough evidence to say social media changes teen health across the whole population. It said social media can both harm and help, and the research often cannot tell which way cause runs.

show.text: Can harm | Can help (for example, connection with friends and family, and support for teens who are ill or grieving)

say.text: Others disagree. A 2026 World Happiness Report chapter argues that social media is harming adolescents at a scale big enough to show up across whole populations.

show.text: National Academies, 2023: not enough evidence yet | World Happiness Report chapter, 2026: harm is large enough to show at population level

ask.q: What did the National Academies committee conclude in 2023?
ask.right: Not enough evidence to say social media changes teen health across the whole population, though it can harm and help
wrong: It was proven to harm every teenager
It was proven to be harmless
The committee did not look at any research
ask.why: The committee said the evidence did not support that conclusion at the population level, and that social media has potential to both harm and benefit.

say.text: Now climate. Weather is what happens today. Climate is the pattern over many years. Climate change means that long pattern is shifting.

show.text: Climate change

say.text: NASA says Earth's average surface temperature has risen about 1 degree Celsius, or 2 Fahrenheit, since the late 1800s. Most of that warming happened in the past 40 years.

show.text: about 1 °C (2 °F) since the late 1800s

say.text: NOAA measures the speed. Warming averaged 0.06 degrees Celsius per decade since 1850, but 0.20 per decade since 1975. That is more than three times faster.

show.text: Warming rate in degrees Celsius per decade

say.text: How do we know? Think back to class one: we read the evidence. Weather stations, ships and buoys tell the recent story. Tree rings, ocean sediments, coral reefs and rock layers tell the older one.

show.text:
Recent: weather stations, ship and buoy measurements
Older: tree rings, ocean sediments, coral reefs, rock layers

say.text: Several groups analyse the temperature separately: NASA, NOAA, Berkeley Earth, the UK Met Office and Copernicus in Europe. Their methods differ, but they show the same ongoing warming trend.

show.text:
NASA
NOAA
Berkeley Earth
UK Met Office (Hadley Centre)
Copernicus (Europe)
Different methods, same trend

ask.q: NASA, NOAA and other groups analyse temperature separately. What do they find?
ask.right: Different methods, but the same ongoing warming trend
wrong: Each finds a different trend, so nobody can tell
They agree only about Europe
They all find the world is cooling
ask.why: NASA reports that the independent groups use different methods and models, yet show the same ongoing warming trend.

say.text: On the cause, NASA says human activity is the principal cause. It quotes the IPCC, which says this has moved from theory to established fact.

show.text: NASA: human activity is the principal cause of the warming.

say.text: Governments responded. In December 2015, 195 nations adopted the Paris Agreement. They aimed to hold warming well below 2 degrees Celsius, and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5.

show.text: December 2015: 195 nations adopt the Paris Agreement | Goal: well below 2 °C, pursue 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels

say.text: Policy is still debated. One source says the agreement sets no quantitative emissions target. A German government agency says it is binding under international law. The IPCC stresses fairness between countries.

show.text: No quantitative emissions target (Asian Development Bank resource) | Binding under international law (German Environment Agency)

ask.q: What temperature goal did the Paris Agreement set?
ask.right: Hold warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5 °C
wrong: Hold warming at exactly 5 °C
Return Earth to its 1850 temperature by 2020
It set no goal and only started a discussion
ask.why: Countries agreed to hold warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

say.text: Now COVID-19. A pandemic is a disease outbreak spreading across many countries at once. COVID-19 is caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2.

show.text: Pandemic

say.text: Cases were first detected in China in December 2019. The World Health Organization declared a global emergency on 30 January 2020, and called it a pandemic on 11 March.

show.text: December 2019: first cases detected in China | 30 January 2020: WHO declares a global health emergency | 11 March 2020: WHO calls it a pandemic

say.text: On 11 March 2020, WHO reported 118,319 confirmed cases and 4,292 deaths. They were spread across 113 countries, territories or areas.

show.text: 118,319 confirmed cases on 11 March 2020

say.text: How many people died? Countries reported 5.42 million deaths in 2020 and 2021. WHO estimates 14.91 million excess deaths in the same two years.

show.text: Reported deaths and estimated excess deaths, 2020-2021

say.text: Excess deaths are deaths above the number expected without the crisis. They include people who died because overstretched hospitals could not treat other illnesses.

show.text: Excess deaths

ask.right: Deaths above the number expected without the crisis
wrong: Only deaths confirmed by a COVID test
Only deaths of people over 60
Only deaths in one country
ask.why: Excess mortality is the difference between the deaths that occurred and the number expected without the crisis. It counts direct and indirect deaths.

say.text: Counts still differ. One summary lists about 7.1 million confirmed deaths but estimates from 18.5 to 35.2 million. WHO ended its emergency in May 2023, yet experts disagree on whether COVID-19 is now pandemic or endemic.

show.text: Confirmed deaths: about 7.1 million | Estimated deaths: 18.5 to 35.2 million

say.text: Last story: artificial intelligence, or AI. It means computer systems that do tasks we link to human thinking, like handling language. Generative AI makes new text, pictures and audio.

show.text: Artificial intelligence (AI)

say.text: In November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot, as a free research preview. From the first day, OpenAI warned it could give plausible-sounding but wrong answers.

show.text: 30 November 2022: ChatGPT released as a free research preview

ask.q: What did OpenAI warn when ChatGPT launched?
ask.right: It could give answers that sound right but are wrong
wrong: It was always correct
It could only be used by scientists
It only worked without the internet
ask.why: OpenAI's first announcement warned that ChatGPT could give plausible-sounding but incorrect answers.

say.text: The Stanford AI Index is an independent yearly report. It found that 78 percent of organizations reported using AI in 2024, up from 55 percent the year before.

show.text: 78% of organizations used AI in 2024 (55% in 2023)

say.text: Governments are reacting too. In 2024, US federal agencies introduced 59 AI-related regulations, more than double the number in 2023.

show.text: 59 US federal AI-related regulations in 2024

say.text: Views differ by place. The report says 80 percent of people in Indonesia think AI products do more good than harm, but only 39 percent in the US. It also says AI still struggles with some complex reasoning tests.

show.text: Indonesia: 80% say AI is more beneficial than harmful | United States: 39% say the same

say.text: Five stories, and none is finished. So why do many historians hesitate to judge the very recent past?

show.text: Why recent history is hard to judge

say.text: Reason one: documents. In Britain, most government papers reach the public only after thirty years. In many countries, government archives stay closed for forty or fifty.

show.text: 30 to 50 years: how long many government archives stay closed

say.text: Reason two: perspective. A historian needs to know what happened next. For recent events, we do not know the consequences yet.

show.text: Perspective

say.text: Reason three: the people involved are alive and may dispute the story. Reason four: today leaves huge amounts of material, which brings its own challenges.

show.text:
1. Documents may still be closed
2. We cannot see the consequences yet
3. The people involved are alive and may disagree
4. A flood of sources is hard to master

ask.q: Which is a reason historians are cautious about the very recent past?
ask.right: Key documents may still be closed, and the consequences are not yet known
wrong: Nothing important has happened recently
Historians are not allowed to study events after the year 2000
Recent events always have complete records
ask.why: Government papers often stay closed for decades, and a clear perspective needs time. Both make recent history harder to judge.

say.text: We saw this today. NASA says 2025 was effectively tied with 2023 as second warmest, behind 2024, while other groups ranked it third. COVID-19 death counts range very widely.

show.text: 2025 temperature: NASA says tied with 2023; other groups say third warmest | COVID-19 deaths: 5.42 million reported vs 14.91 million estimated (2020-21)

say.text: Not every historian agrees we should wait. Two historians note that the recent past is where lessons matter most, yet gets the least attention. A growing number now write recent history.

show.text: Wait: documents and distance first | Do not wait: recent history matters and others will fill the gap

say.text: So hold facts firmly and conclusions loosely. Next time, our final class looks ahead to the future of Earth and the universe.

show.text: Facts firmly, conclusions loosely

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Bear Stearns was bought by JPMorgan Chase in spring 2008. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September, and the Fed approved an $85 billion loan to AIG the next day.
Pew ran its first survey of smartphone ownership. It found 35 percent of US adults owned one.
195 nations adopted the Paris Agreement on climate change at COP21.
WHO declared a global health emergency on 30 January and called COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March. That day it counted 118,319 confirmed cases in 113 countries, territories or areas.
OpenAI released ChatGPT as a free research preview.
NOAA reports 2024 as the warmest year since global records began in 1850. In the same year, 78 percent of organizations reported using AI.
NASA found 2025 effectively tied with 2023 for warmest year, while other groups ranked it third warmest.

other_side.claim: Letting Lehman Brothers fail caused the 2008 panic, or was the key mistake.
other_side.other_view: Fed Chair Ben Bernanke indicated the Fed could not lend safely because Lehman lacked enough good collateral. A Wharton timeline notes that the bankruptcy's significance is disputed, and the New York Fed describes a Panic of 2007 that was already under way before Lehman.

other_side.claim: Social media is not shown to change teen mental health across the whole population (National Academies, 2023).
other_side.other_view: A 2026 World Happiness Report chapter argues that social media is harming adolescents at a scale large enough to show up at the population level. The National Academies also noted that much research cannot tell which way cause runs, and that social media has benefits for some teens.

other_side.claim: The Paris Agreement is a binding treaty that drives emissions cuts.
other_side.other_view: One resource notes it sets no quantitative emission reduction target. A German government agency says it is binding under international law. The IPCC stresses that equity between countries is part of the debate.
WHO ended its public health emergency in May 2023 but said COVID-19 remained a global health threat. Time reported that expert opinions differ on whether it is now endemic or still pandemic.

other_side.claim: People are broadly positive about AI.
other_side.other_view: The Stanford AI Index reports big regional differences: 80 percent of people surveyed in Indonesia say AI products are more beneficial than harmful, against 39 percent in the US. It also notes that AI still struggles with some complex reasoning tests.

other_side.claim: Historians should wait decades before writing about recent events.
other_side.other_view: Hennessy and Seldon say the recent past is where lessons would be most useful, yet gets the least attention. History News Network authors say a growing number of historians now write about the recent past. An American Historical Association essay adds that such work brings practical and moral dilemmas, such as closed archives and ethics.
